There is a minor problem when updating the firmware over MQTT which causes exception if you don't follow the protocol properly and try to upload the very same firmware twice in a row.

- board will respond with homie/<deviceid>/$implementation/ota/status 304
- ignore the error and send the firmware to homie/<deviceid>/$implementation/ota/firmware anyway
- the board will print to console "Receiving OTA firmware but not requested, skipping..."

body:
AsyncMqttClient v0.7.0 `publish` returns `0` if there's not enough space for a packet to be sent.

title: Homie 2.0 remains forever waiting for Wi-Fi connection
body:
I have a Homie node in operation (boot normal mode) working ok. If I press the RESET button in the ESP8266 the firmware restarts. After the initial debug messages Homie attempts to connect to WiFi but it remains there forever. This is the last debug message:

↕ Attempting to connect to Wi-Fi...

After several hours of investigation I've discovered that if I remove power supply from ESP8266, wait for a couple of minutes and power it up again, now the node works ok. It looks as if Homie get stacked in a wait loop for the wifi connection event, but this event never takes place because the wifi connection still exists (probably, the time required to reset the system is so small than the WiFi station didn't notice that the ESP8266 was disconnected and so the wifi connection was not dropped. And when the ESP8266 asks to connect to wifi it never receives a new connection as it still exists. Not sure if this is the cause but it is the only explanation I have. But I don't know how to fix this behaviour. 

I also have noticed this problem when the node is in operation and I upload a new firmware (direct upload, not using OTA). After the upload is finished, ESP8266 automatically restarts and the new firmware is executed (boot normal mode). Homie attempts to connect to WiFi but it remains there forever. And the only solution is to remove power supply for a couple of minutes.

I'm using Homie 2.0 from development repo.

title: Reject ota/firmware only once (vs. with every payload chunk)
body:
If an OTA server publishes firmware to `$implementation/ota/firmware`
- to a Homie device with OTA disabled, or 
- without having sent a new firmware version to `$ota` first

then Homie replies `403` (forbidden) or `400 NOT_REQUESTED` status for every chunk of payload it receives (which is about 350 times for a simple firmware).

This PR makes Homie reply only once per MQTT message.

title: Bugfix base64-encoded firmware when (size mod 3) equals 1
body:
I noticed an issue with base64-encoded OTA updates: for some firmware base-encoded OTA update worked and for some it didn't.

It turned out that, if the real firmware size modulo 3 equaled 1, firmware was incorrectly rejected with `400 BAD_FIRMWARE`. The reason was that the code I added only expected the real firmware size to be off by **one** from the "guestimated" size (3/4 ratio of the total length of the `=` padded base64 payload). However, the real firmware size may as well be off by **two** from the 3/4 ratio.

Examples with some realistic firmware sizes:

| Real firmware size | Real size modulo 3 | Base64 length | Base64 Padding | Estimated firmware size | Size off-by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 346992 | 0 | 462656 | (none) | 346992 | 0 |
| 346993 | 1 | 462660 | "==" | 346995 | 2 |
| 346994 | 2 | 462660 | "=" | 346995 | 1 |
| 346995 | 0 | 462660 | (none) | 346995 | 0 |
| 346996 | 1 | 462664 | "==" | 346998 | 2 |
| 346997 | 2 | 462664 | "=" | 346998 | 1 |
| 346998 | 0 | 462664 | (none) | 346998 | 0 |

Or, more general (N = any natural number):

| Real firmware size | Real size modulo 3 | Base64 length | Base64 Padding | Estimated firmware size | Size off-by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| N*3 | 0 | N*4 | (none) | N*3 | 0 |
| N*3+1 | 1 | (N+1)*4 | "==" | N*3+1 | 2 |
| N*3+2 | 2 | (N+1)*4 | "=" | N*3+1 | 1 |

This PR fixes the base64 length issue. In addition, the PR adds a check for payload size evenly dividable by 4 with base64-encoded payloads.

title: Fix #589: ota-updater.py for V2 and V3 devices
body:
One line to fix both problems mentioned in #589:

Checking the "$state" topic for not "false" was wrong, because since v3
the online state must be "ready" to continue.

Thus, also in "init" state the ota-updater re-subscribed to the $fw
topic and thus got old retained checksum from broker. (The homie device
usually has not sent the new $fw/checksum at this moment).

Now the script uses the firmware MD5 only if it has been sent from a
"ready" device (or $online != false device to support v2.x devices).

title: Humidity is disabled in the BME280 I2C driver because of a missing write operation
body:
Calling the `Humidity()` function on the `BME280Driver` I2C driver results in the error: "Humidity disabled".

This is because the `initHumidity()` function is incomplete; it writes out the humidity data acquisition options, but doesn't then write to the "ctrl_meas" register, as per Section 5.4.3 of the BME280 data sheet:

> The “ctrl_hum” register sets the humidity data acquisition options of the device. Changes to
> this register only become effective after a write operation to “ctrl_meas”.

I have a patch so can generate a pull request if someone else can confirm that this is the case! I have tested this on a Raspberry Pi Model B using the Sparkfun BME280 Atmospheric Sensor Breakout with gobot 1.5.0 and golang 1.7.5.

Device bulk operations, such as apiClient.deleteMultipleDevices() will throw an "com.ibm.iotf.client.IoTFCReSTException: Some devices deleted successfully" exception when the status code is 202 even if all of the devices were processed succesfully.
See: https://docs.internetofthings.ibmcloud.com/apis/swagger/v0002/org-admin.html#!/Device_Bulk_Configuration

[

title: Cannot listen on gateway metadata changes
Connect timeout problems
body:
https://github.com/ibm-watson-iot/iot-java/blob/e1a2f9184fe28829ba69f67230b2cdc13ba2a693/src/main/java/com/ibm/wiotp/sdk/AbstractClient.java#L117

We need to fix the timeout handling on connect:

```
MqttConnectOptions options = config.getMqttConnectOptions();
mqttAsyncClient.connect(options).waitForCompletion(DEFAULT_ACTION_TIMEOUT);
```

`DEFAULT_ACTION_TIMEOUT` is 5 seconds (and is fine for publishes/subscribes etc) ... but is also being used for the connect, which can take more than 5s in some network conditions.

In https://github.com/ibm-watson-iot/iot-java/blob/e1a2f9184fe28829ba69f67230b2cdc13ba2a693/src/main/java/com/ibm/wiotp/sdk/device/config/DeviceConfig.java#L91 (and similar config classes) we set the connection timeout in paho to 60 seconds.

Let's set the timeout we use on this wait to slightly longer than the paho timeout -- 80 seconds, so that the wait does not timeout while paho is still trying to connect, and will only fire if something has gone wrong and paho hasn't itself timed out and returned by the time it should have done so.

While we're at it, let's also increase public static final long `DEFAULT_ACTION_TIMEOUT` to 10 seconds, if network is going heroicly slow it's better to cater to this, there's no real benefit to giving up 5 seconds earlier.

title: Enforce value constraints in Characteristic. Distinguish raw and HAP value.
body:
Currently, Characteristic only respects min/max value constraints when sending its state through the `to_HAP` method. However, when a value change is published to iOS clients (`notify`), the sent value could be outside of min/max range. There should be a distinction between actual char value and it's "hap" representation, .e.g:
```python
char = Characteristic(...)
char.value  # raw value
char.get_value()  # hapified value
char.set_value(value, ...)
# ^ should be equivalent to
if value not in self.allowed_values: raise ....
self.value = value
```

title: WiFi Reconnect Issues
body:
I've had to power of/ on my thermostat a couple of times in the last 3 months as it has dropped off the network and never reconnects (MQTT messages stop working/ there is no assigned DHCP lease etc). I suspect my automated AP firmware update causes the wireless to disconnect, but the thermostat simply never reconnects and is the only IOT device (of about 30) that doesn't. No SoftAP etc, it's just offline.

The thermostat itself works, in that the relay is triggered at target temperature and the target temperature can be adjusted.

Not sure if it matters but I tend to run with webServer set to false.

Is there any way to increase logging/ send serial logs to MQTT or another source? 

Has anyone else experience issues such as this?
symptom: Message delivery issues, Reconnection issues, Disconnetion issues, Firmware update issues

**What would you like to be added**:

title: race condition @ DTContext.Lock / DTContext.Unlock
body:
**What happened**:
We have a potential race @ locking / unlocking the device mutex. (https://github.com/kubeedge/kubeedge/blob/0ddc4b3f7752fb527c73bec4d5d2adbe5f3635f2/edge/pkg/devicetwin/dtcontext/dtcontext.go#L107-L128)

EXAMPLE CASE:
- 2 messages from the same device
- start handling first message
  - run dtc.Lock('xyz')
      - success on dtc.Mutex.Lock()
      - success on deviceMutex.Lock()
      - success on dtc.Mutex.Unlock()
- start handling second message
   - run dtc.Lock('xyz')
      - success on dtc.Mutex.Lock()
      - bounded waiting on deviceMutex.Lock() # beause the first message has this mutex
- continue handling first message
  - run dtc.Unlock('xyz')
     - bounded waiting on dtc.Mutex.Unlock() # because the second message has the mutex

**What you expected to happen**:
no race condition

title: Improve URI validator
body:
Right now the URI validator we have created works both for one URI (String) and a list of URIs (Array). To make the validator complete you must be able to set an optional parameter to set the fact that the field can accept URIs or an URI.

Something like this should work.
`validates list: uri: {array: true}   # accept list of uris`

This is needed because if later on we want to make a check on the URI to extract something we could have some errors and it would be better to find it before. If we do not have this validation option we could send an array of URIs where only one can be accepted and have unexpected errors.

body: Create all types defined in the icon document and test their functionalities in the dashboard. You need to check how everything works out. To make this possible you first need to close all types issues on this milestone and to deploy Lelylan Types dashboard.

title: Change URIs to IDs
body: All connections and all definitions must be made through IDs and not URIs as it makes things overcomplicated without a read gain. You need to revisit the whole logic and the whole documentation in the Dev Center

title: Type family
body: Every device must be part of a family of device. There will be different types of lights but they will always be **lights**. You need to add a predefined (in possibilities of selections) family that identify a type and that is then passed to the device. Think if you need a tagging like system or if a device belong to a unique family. Probably the latter is the right one, and for other cases we can use groups.

title: Resource owner id
body:
Add resource_owner_id to all models. Remove created_from.
- location
- type
- device

title: Device contained in
body: A device must be capable to easily get all the groups and locations it belongs to. We could make it through the client by preloading all locations and groups and later on by checking in which locations and groups a device is included. Another solution is to add this info directly to the device. Think which one is the best solution for all sceneries.

title: Property type
body: Add a #type to every property where you can set the UI format of the property. For example `color`, `range`, `number`, `text` (default) and based on this type you can have an array, an hash or anything as accepted values.

title: Add a default function to status
body: Every status can have a default function. This function can be used to get a direct way to interact with the device. Usually the function is a basic one and is ON/OFF. Think if we can have this also without the usage of statuses. They are pretty complex and we are thinking about removing them.

title: Telecom
body: Close with Telecom contract giving them all code till 2 years ago..

title: BundleAdmin: stop does not stop dependencies
body: When stopping a bundle in the macchina.io webui BundleAdmin app, all bundles dependent upon that bundle should also be stopped, as in the old OSP BundleAdmin tool.

title: OSP Web Server: clear cache when bundle is removed
body: Static resources in the in-memory OSP Web Server cache must be removed when the bundle providing them is removed. Currently they stay in the cache, which leads to old data being served when a bundle is upgraded.

Typical mainflux docker-compose setup

title: gRPC Load Balancing between http-adapter and things
body:
**BUG REPORT** 

1. What were you trying to achieve?
Targeted TPS load testing against http-adapter and a failure scenario

2. What are the expected results?
balanced, self-healing connections between mainflux components

3. What are the received results?
gRPC not being load balanced, and when a pod is killed, these connections are not rebalanced

4. What are the steps to reproduce the issue?
- Run a load test in kubernetes with multiple replicas (http-adapter is using the `things` service name as url)
- Note that the majority of transactions are running through a single `things` pod and not load balanced
- Kill the `things` pod that's receiving the majority of transations
- Note the error rate spikes and connections from adapter to things remain in error and are not rebalanced.

5. In what environment did you encounter the issue?
kubernetes 

6. Additional information you deem important:
This might be slightly out of scope, as it's possible to solve this with Istio/Linkerd or some k8s ingress that is aware of gRPC. But want to bring it up as it looks like you're exploring similar replacements for nginx.

title: Values of zero are being omitted
body: **(Semi) BUG REPORT** Noticed this when the value field wasn't being written out onto a kafka topic. This may be more of an issue with what protoc generates but I believe Mainflux should account for this. So I wanted to just make sure you all were aware it. 1. What were you trying to achieve? Sending a message where the value is zero. 2. What are the expected results? That the `value` field does not get omitted and contains a value of zero when the message that is sent contains 0. 3. What are the received results? The value field gets omitted and is non-existent rather than zero 4. What are the steps to reproduce the issue? The way I found easiest to visualize this, was through subscribing to the NATS channel where the normalized messages are written to (out.senml for example) and then decoding the messages. - Sub to out.senml and capture the output. - Send a message containing a zero for the value for example: ``` [ { "bn":"MVP-mikes-fridge-sensor:", "bt":1537822790, "bu":"degC", "bver":5, "n":"Temperature", "u":"degC", "v":0 } ] ``` - Decode that output using protoc and although a value was sent, it does not appear What I am seeing when I do this: 5. In what environment did you encounter the issue? Kubernetes 6. Additional information you deem important: I believe that a Zero value should be valid and not get omitted anywhere in Mainflux. Since things like refrigerators/freezers can send temperatures that are 0. The issue probably truly lies in protoc/go since protoc generates message.pg.go: ``` type Message struct { ... Value float64 `protobuf:"fixed64,6,opt,name=Value,proto3" json:"Value,omitempty"` ... } ``` Due to a combination of omitempty getting added and zero being considered empty in go, the `Value` field does not get populated. Let me know thoughts about this!

title: `device` deletion should trigger referencing `channel`s deletions
body:
Current `device` model (https://github.com/Mainflux/mainflux-lite/blob/master/models/device.go, https://github.com/Mainflux/mainflux-lite/blob/master/models/deviceTemplate.json) has no reference to `channel`s created for this device - only `channel` holds the referenced device `Device` ID: https://github.com/Mainflux/mainflux-lite/blob/master/models/channel.go, https://github.com/Mainflux/mainflux-lite/blob/master/models/channelTemplate.json

`channel` is accessed as `localhost:7070/devices/<device_id>/channels/<channel_id>`. When DELETE is issued on this URI, channel will be deleted. However - when DELETE is issued on `localhost:7070/devices/<device_id>` only device will be deleted, but not the channels that belog to this device - and we will not be able to access them anymore (since we will not have ID of the device anymore).

Do we have to keep list of `channels` in `device` struct? Xively holds the array `channels` inside `device`: http://developer.xively.com/assets/Xively_QS_TimeSeries.pdf. Not sure how M2X does it, but it is worh looking: https://m2x.att.com/developer/documentation/v2/device

title: Correct usage of docker persistent volumes
body:
As I was working on #636 I've noticed that some volumes are generated when executing `docker-compose`.

I've dug a bit deeper and I've found out that we're already using volumes for the users-db, things-db, mainflux-redis, mainflux-things-redis, bootstrap, influxdb-writer, cassandra-writer, mongodb-writer containers, but we delete them with `make cleandocker` and `make cleanghost`.

Here is the test procedure:

1. start from clear state

```
$ make cleandocker

$ docker volume ls
DRIVER              VOLUME NAME
```

2. start Mainflux
```
$	docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d (equivalent to make run)
```
3. the state with the volumes afterwards:
```
$ docker volume ls
DRIVER              VOLUME NAME
local               18f49a276e35cc4ad115ecefd638a1b594538b7abe117d4abb2ee9ce60700231
local               264a2c95f31d7d51291ef9cca2294d017d51c5961e421a2e35797ee070505172

local               d5886127963d2728dd2d3e7b31c4f4ad66ffa135550c2fce633ab0f342177832
```

4. find the containers to which these volumes belong to: `docker ps --filter=volume=<VOLUME_NAME>`
```
$ docker ps --filter=volume=18f49a276e35cc4ad115ecefd638a1b594538b7abe117d4abb2ee9ce60700231 --filter=volume=264a2c95f31d7d51291ef9cca2294d017d51c5961e421a2e35797ee070505172 --filter=volume=c2442c40d8dca66ae9f96ff5c438417d6a12f19f56b3f03501d3b3a129b41c3d --filter=volume=d5886127963d2728dd2d3e7b31c4f4ad66ffa135550c2fce633ab0f342177832
CONTAINER ID        IMAGE                  COMMAND                  CREATED             STATUS              PORTS               NAMES
0e0dd71e5174        postgres:10.2-alpine   "docker-entrypoint.s…"   19 minutes ago      Up 19 minutes       5432/tcp            mainflux-things-db
039b13ffd155        redis:4.0.9-alpine     "docker-entrypoint.s…"   19 minutes ago      Up 19 minutes       6379/tcp            mainflux-redis
2e4188a46327        postgres:10.2-alpine   "docker-entrypoint.s…"   19 minutes ago      Up 19 minutes       5432/tcp            mainflux-users-db
bdde4c8e5f25        redis:5.0-alpine       "docker-entrypoint.s…"   19 minutes ago      Up 19 minutes       6379/tcp            mainflux-things-redis
```

5. The existence of the volumes can be easily confirmed by checking the Dockerfiles from which the docker hub images are build:

* Postgres 10.2-alpine  [Dockerfile](https://github.com/docker-library/postgres/blob/master/10/alpine/Dockerfile#L145)
* Redis 5.0-alpine [Dockerfile](https://github.com/docker-library/redis/blob/60db7082c81f5d457046f199244c5d651f04b3fa/5.0/alpine/Dockerfile#L60)
* Redis 4.0.9-alpine  [Dockerfile](https://github.com/docker-library/redis/blob/8e1acc18156603cc3643bf22ced6069cf8be1622/4.0/alpine/Dockerfile#L60)
* Cassandra [Dockerfile](https://github.com/docker-library/cassandra/blob/064fb4e2682bf9c1909e4cb27225fa74862c9086/3.11/Dockerfile#L156)
* InfluxDB [Dockerfile](https://github.com/influxdata/influxdata-docker/blob/d76a6a184dec6a82978964882641a743adb76989/influxdb/1.6/alpine/Dockerfile#L31)
* MongoDB [Dockerfile](https://github.com/docker-library/mongo/blob/7276b14c1e9b5f83b37f5f452e6a9f293aea2d8b/3.6/Dockerfile#L90)
* Grafana [recommended setup](http://docs.grafana.org/installation/docker/#grafana-container-with-persistent-storage-recommended)




6. cleaning up the docker containers
```
make cleandocker
```
this make task calls the `cleanghost` task which contains a `docker volume ls -f dangling=true -q | xargs -r docker volume rm` commands which deletes all the dangling volumes. __The problem is that it deletes all__ dangling volumes, volumes not connected to any container. IMHO this is totally wrong. We should only delete the containers which we have created and not all of the dangling containers which means we might delete some oder important data from other containers. The __second problem__ is that the deletion of the dangling containers happens before the Mainflux containers are stopped and removed so we leave some "garbage" behind. If a new composition is executed there will be 8 volumes which are created by us. The volumes from ther previous composition are deleted on the second run of `cleandocker` or `cleanghost`
In fact, the whole `cleanghost` target does not check if the containers, images or volumes are created by us or not, but it simply deletes them all.

__The solution__ for this problem would be to use names for the volumes so that we can filter them easier, clearly show which volumes were created by us and delete only these volumes and add filters to all of the `cleanghost` commands. We should also add a switch which will tell if the volumes should be deleted or not. The default behavior should be the same as now, when the switch is not present the `cleandocker` and `cleanghost` make task should delete the volumes.

Also, having proper names for the volumes makes it straightforward to backup and restore them without too much hassle and playing around with to many docker commands ;)

Although this is more an enhancement, I've marked it as as bug as well, as we delete all exited contaniers and unused images instead of deleting only the things that we have created

My sensors publish SenML json data via MQTT to the assigned channel. This works as expected. The data is also normalized and written into the InfluxDB via the influxdb-writer.

body:
Adapters should not try to normalize SenML - they must forward "as-is" messages to NATS for other adapters to re-publish them to their subscribers.

Also, new microservice that normalizes SenML should be created as NodeJS does not have appropriate SenML processing libraries.

Finally, normalizes SenML should also be published on a separate topic, fro `message-writer` to consume it (as it expects a array of normalized SenML messages).

Publishing SenML/CBOR topic looking like `[{0: "TST", 4: true}]`  in CBOR diagnostic notation (`81 a2 00 63 54 53 54 04 f5`) causes runtime error in normalizer.
Fix me, but I am sure that the message conforms [RFC 8428](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8428).  
```bash
mainflux-mqtt   | {"level":30,"time":1573140521695,"msg":"published","pid":1,"hostname":"34e546c4ae1a","client":{"id":"GlobalClient"},"message":{"topic":"channels/1531a2f3-5a2a-4404-a168-cad5ea289d4c/messages/ct/application_senml-cbor","qos":0,"retain":false},"v":1}
mainflux-normalizer | {"level":"warn","message":"Method normalize took 46.934µs to complete with error: cbor decode error [pos 3]: runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0.","ts":"2019-11-07T15:28:41.695720118Z"}
```

On the other hand  the message encoded as
```bash
[{"n": "TST", "vb": true}]
81         # array(1)
A2         # map(2)
61         # text(1)
6E         # "n"
63         # text(3)
545354     #"TST"
62         # text(2)
7662       # "vb"
F5         # primitive(21)
```
is processed fine.
Seems there is RFC 8428 violation bug in https://github.com/cisco/senml + https://github.com/ugorji/go . See  "RFC 8428 (August 2018) Jennings, et al. Standards Track [Page 19]"

title: The node.js not in the system PATH env
body: I had another attendee where they installed node.js via the devkit, however it would never resolve inside the VS Code integrated terminal (even after closing and restarting VS code).  I had her manually install node from the web site, making sure to include Node in the path, and that fixed it.

title: Update IoT Hub installer such that it works for users who only have resource group-level access
body:
The IoT development kit includes tasks that are added to Visual Studio Code that will deploy an IoT Hub into Azure. If the user you use to connect into Azure while following these tasks only has resource group-level access (i.e. no subscription access), the deployment will fail unnecessarily because it will attempt to register the Microsoft.Devices resource provider even if it is already registered in the subscription, in the context of a user who only has resource group-level access.

The root issue lies on line 21 of task-iothub.js. Instead of lazily assuming you are a subscription admin and forcing the registration of the Microsoft.Devices resource provider, the logic should check to see if the Microsoft.Devices resource provider is already registered or not before attempting to register the resource provider. This approach allows a subscription admin to register the Microsoft.Devices resource provider so that other users who do not have that level of access can successfully deploy IoT Hubs into the resource groups where they have access.

To fix this, replace this line (line 21):

```javascript
_context.next = 7;return azurecli.exec('provider register -n "Microsoft.Devices"');case 7:
```

With the following lines:

```javascript
_context.next = 5;return (azurecli.execResultJson('provider show -n "Microsoft.Devices"')); case 5:
devicesProvider = _context.sent;_context.next = 7;if (devicesProvider.registrationState === 'NotRegistered') {
    console.log('Registering resource provider "Microsoft.Devices" in subscription ' + context.subscription);
    return azurecli.exec('provider register -n "Microsoft.Devices"')};break;case 7:
```

I would have made these changes in a PR myself, but @ArthurMa1978 informed me on Gitter that the task part of the device SDK is not open source at the moment and requested I log the issue here so that it can be addressed in the new VS Code extension that is coming soon. I already made these changes locally and it seems to work just fine using a user who only has contributor access to a single resource group in Azure, with no subscription-level permissions at all.

title: Toolkit-timer: 'delay' parameter is not respected after first use and in stopped state
body:
The toolkit Timer uses *firstDelay* and *interval* parameters to control the timer behaviour. If the timer is stopped and the delay is ever re-set using **setDelay** or **setDelayAndInterval** methods, only the *interval* part is respected when the timer is restarted.

Note, that when the timer is in a running state, the methods correctly behave as expected (both are respected).

Correct behaviour would be for both parameters to be respected whether in a running or stopped state, with *firstDelay* reset every time a **setDelay___** function is used.

Tip: It's the step after the last dot that caused this error, not those before it.
----
Tip: If the failing expression is known to be legally refer to something that's sometimes null or missing, either specify a default value like myOptionalVar!myDefault, or use <#if myOptionalVar??>when-present<#else>when-missing. title: Activate command for nRF24L01 toggles plus features
body:
According to the nRF24L01 datasheet (non-plus!) the ACTIVATE command toggles advanced features each time it is called:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7716005/43391165-3c7073b2-93f0-11e8-888b-27b83612b5c6.png)

We must make sure the radio is in a default state, with ACTIVATE features switched off before executing the ACTIVATE command.
Currently, the RF24_enableFeatures() call (which executes the ACTIVATE command) is called from setup with the radio in Standby-I mode:
https://github.com/mysensors/MySensors/blob/development/drivers/RF24/RF24.cpp#L506

It is likely that the radio has to be brought to PowerDown mode, or even power cycled to get to a defined ACTIVATE state.

I don't have non-plus radios available. Can someone verify if current implementation toggles the  advanced feature availibility?

title: pinIntTrigger should be made volatile

title: presentNode is not called on gateway with only local sensors
body:
On gateway with only local sensors, without `MY_RADIO_FEATURE`, `presentNode` is not called. This breaks the API specification and controllers will have a hard time registering the local sensors if the parent node is missing.

Bug reported from user of home assistant controller in pymysensors repo:
https://github.com/theolind/pymysensors/issues/51

and in the forum:
https://forum.mysensors.org/topic/4276/converting-a-sketch-from-1-5-x-to-2-0-x/2

The relevant parts of the code:
https://github.com/mysensors/MySensors/blob/986389b12591917ecbc44021c63a2cdf6f8c8222/MySensors.h#L56-L58

https://github.com/mysensors/MySensors/blob/986389b12591917ecbc44021c63a2cdf6f8c8222/core/MySensorsCore.cpp#L152-L154

https://github.com/mysensors/MySensors/blob/934ccf30b205afad2086c908a367c4205ce580cd/core/MySensorsCore.cpp#L181-L190

https://github.com/mysensors/MySensors/blob/934ccf30b205afad2086c908a367c4205ce580cd/core/MySensorsCore.cpp#L325-L329

A temporary workaround is to call `present` with child id 255 directly in the sketch in `setup`:

```
void setup() {
  // Present node as repeater node.
  present(255, 18);
}
```

My suggestion is to move the check for `MY_RADIO_FEATURE` to somewhere here:
https://github.com/mysensors/MySensors/blob/934ccf30b205afad2086c908a367c4205ce580cd/core/MySensorsCore.cpp#L192-L213

I don't know exactly what calls in that section needs a radio, so if someone can advise or hint where to look, I can push a PR more quickly.

title: AVR: Pin interrupt may not get detached after calling hwSleep
body:
When calling the hwSleep() variant taking 1 or 2 pin interrupts, the pin interrupt(s) are not detached on return in the following cases:
1. Wake by timeout: no interrupt(s) detached
2. Wake by pin interrupt: in case hwSleep is called with 2 pin interrupts, the interrupt that didn't occur does not get detached.

A pin interrupt that did not get detached will be detached the next time it occurs.

title: AVR might sleep with interrupts disabled
body:
See potential issue here: http://playground.arduino.cc/Learning/ArduinoSleepCode

MySensors interrupt handlers for sleep (wakeUp1() & wakeUp2()) should disable sleep, by adding a call to sleep_disable()

title: AVR might wake from pending external interrupt
body:
Pending external interrupts are not cleared when attaching an interrupt handler.
This might cause an AVR to immediately wake up again when going to sleep, without an interrupt actually triggering the wake.
Ref: https://forum.arduino.cc/index.php?topic=59217.0

title: AVR Sleep times deviate from watchdog timer
body:
For sleep times <= 125ms the breakdown into individual watchdog timeout intervals is wrong.
This might cause deviation of actual sleep time from requested sleep time.

## Description of the problem :

During the association, **randomly**, the sensor receives an ID longer than the 3 characters of range 0-255 normally expected.

These are often numbers 255 or 100 placed after the ID, other numbers appear or changes the ID itself, but this is more rare.

In the example below, the good ID sent by the gateway is 197, the sensor receives 197255 and takes ID 135 after conversion:
197255 = b110000001010000111, converted to uint8, only the last 8 bits on the right (b010000111) are retrieved, giving 135.

### For information, here is the topology of the network setup:

![img_0931](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4836635/30483613-c7ca5586-9a27-11e7-846d-1b4640149b0c.jpg)


## Proposed amendment to the code:

I have not yet figured out the exact origin of the problem, however it seems to me it would be a good idea that the protocol is resistant to this ID corruption:

In the transportAssignNodeID function of MyTransport.cpp, the test:
```
// verify if ID valid
if (newNodeId! = GATEWAY_ADDRESS && newNodeId <= AUTO) {
```
Replacing "! =" With "<=" is not enough because the conversion to uint8 returns a pseudo-random number when the ID is greater than 255;

Change to uint32 type rather than uint8 works but is not optimized and could result many side-effects.

I propose this modification based on the length of the message which has the advantage of not touching the statement of the function:

### Before:
```
bool transportAssignNodeID(const uint8_t newNodeId)
{
	// verify if ID valid
	if (newNodeId != GATEWAY_ADDRESS && newNodeId != AUTO) {
		_transportConfig.nodeId = newNodeId;
		transportSetAddress(newNodeId);
		// Write ID to EEPROM
		hwWriteConfig(EEPROM_NODE_ID_ADDRESS, newNodeId);
		TRANSPORT_DEBUG(PSTR("TSF:SID:OK,ID=%d\n"),newNodeId);	// Node ID assigned
		return true;
	} else {
		TRANSPORT_DEBUG(PSTR("!TSF:SID:FAIL,ID=%d\n"),newNodeId);	// ID is invalid, cannot assign ID
		setIndication(INDICATION_ERR_NET_FULL);
		_transportConfig.nodeId = AUTO;
		return false;
	}
}
```

### After:
```
bool transportAssignNodeID(const uint8_t newNodeId)
{
	// verify if ID corrupted
	if(mGetLength(_msg) <= 3) {
		// verify if ID valid
		if (newNodeId != GATEWAY_ADDRESS && newNodeId <= AUTO) {
			_transportConfig.nodeId = newNodeId;
			transportSetAddress(newNodeId);
			// Write ID to EEPROM
			hwWriteConfig(EEPROM_NODE_ID_ADDRESS, newNodeId);
			TRANSPORT_DEBUG(PSTR("TSF:SID:OK,ID=%d\n"),newNodeId);	// Node ID assigned
			return true;
		}
		TRANSPORT_DEBUG(PSTR("!TSF:SID:FAIL,ID=%d\n"),newNodeId);	// ID is invalid, cannot assign ID
	} else {
		TRANSPORT_DEBUG(PSTR("!TSF:SID:FAIL,CORRUPT\n"),newNodeId);	// ID is corrupted, cannot assign ID
	}
	setIndication(INDICATION_ERR_NET_FULL);
	_transportConfig.nodeId = AUTO;
	return false;
}
```

title: SensorSwitch::onInterrupt() doesn't reliably detect rising/falling edge
body:
The issue is that there is a delay between the interrupt being triggered, and when this line of code executes:

https://github.com/mysensors/NodeManager/blob/4525b56f642d5996035f732a5a383ded59cdb9ed/NodeManagerLibrary.ino#L1549

The delay is typically 2ms if SERVICE_MESSAGES is not enabled, and 200-1500ms if SERVICE_MESSAGES is enabled. 

Say `_mode==FALLING`, and the pin receives a very brief pulse (e.g. a very brief push of a button); by the time this line of code runs the input may have gone high again, so `(_mode == FALLING && value == LOW)` will return false, and the method will interpret this as an invalid value.

My use case is a push button where I want to measure the length of time the button was pressed for. I've created a custom sensor that subclasses SensorSwitch; in the onInterrupt() method I need to be able to reliably tell whether the interrupt was triggered by a FALLING edge (button pushed) or a RISING edge (button released), even if the button was pushed so briefly that the pulse is only a few ms long. 

I believe the only reliable way to detect whether a CHANGE interrupt was triggered by a RISING or FALLING edge is to read the pin as the very first instruction in the ISR (and store it somewhere for later use). 

Apologies if that doesn't make sense (struggling with words today), happy to clarify if needed.

title: SensorDs18b20::_getAddress(int index)  attempts to write into protected string constant on STM32
body:
I found out why the Ds18b20 routines were crashing on my HyTiny board and I *think* why they were working on the Arduino, apparently the STM32 has memory protection for string constants so using the statement char* charAddr = (char*)"                "; to allocate writeable string space doesn't work -- I'm guessing the Arduino processors don't and let you write into the constant.

I changed the statement to char* charAddr = new char[20]; and now the HyTiny is up and running and reporting temperature.   Now I see why it worked in the non-dev version and why I was seeing it work on the other boards.   

I'm not sure if new char[20] is the best way to allocate the storage but for now it has me back up and running.

title: Issue with FEATURE_CONDITIONAL_REPORT with interrupt
body:
I have a battery powered node with a BH1750 sensor for which I have set conditional reporting as follows:

`light.children.get(1)->setValueDelta(2);
  light.children.get(1)->setForceUpdateMinutes(25);`

Attached to the same node I have a SensorDoor using interrupts. I had a problem when only rising changes were being sent back to the controller. The interrupt would fire and pre-post sleep messages would be sent but the actual payload:0 message would never be sent. If FEATURE_CONDITIONAL_REPORT was disabled it would work properly.

I tracked it down to _min_threshold var being set to FLT_MIN which comes up as 0. This meant the 0 value was being filtered out in the ChildInt::sendValue(bool force) method.
I set this in my node code:
`door.children.get(1)->setMinThreshold(-FLT_MIN);`
This resolves the issue. 
But probably that was not how this function was intended. Aware you are mid-way through a rewrite so maybe this doesn't apply any more but thought I'd point it out anyway as took some tracking down!

title: Display update of SSD1306 broken in latest version
body:
In the latest development version, a SSD1306 display will NOT update its texts. The reason is that in Sensor::loop the check 
    	if (_evaluateTimer(_measure_timer) || message != nullptr) {
will never return true, because the timer is explicitly set not to trigger at all in the OLED display's constructor. So by default, the display will update once (when _first_run == false) and then never again.

Since Sensor::loop is not virtual, I also don't see any chance in a Display object to override the loop behaviour, either.

In previous versions, I could add a Child to cause the check in the loop to evaluate to true. However, this has changed in the latest development version and an existing child no longer forces the onLoop function to be called at all. This makes sense, but it breaks the workaround I had to use to make the OLED update so far.

Any idea how to make the OLED displays update, while not sending data to the gateway for them?

title: CONDITIONAL_REPORT in conjunction with setvaluedelta causes the value to never be transferred
NRF51 implementation has millis() wrap around after ~38 hours, timer no longer triggers
body:
The NRF51 core implementation has a millis() counter that wraps around after ~38 hours. 

Unfortunately, after the wrap-around the main loop is still called, but each sensor's timer will never expire, because in Timer::isOver()
    		if (millis() > _target) return true;
will never match. The _target will be set to a value larger than the wrap-around.

The Timer::isOver function needs to add a detection for millis() wrap around for implementations that do not use the full value range of unsigned long...

title: Unable to add Things via text config after they previously removed
body:
I noticed a problem in OpenHAB2.5.0M1 & OpenHAB2.5.0M2.

When commenting out a 'Thing' via a text file and later re-adding that same 'Thing' by removing the comments - the text file gets parsed correctly but the 'Thing' is never created (again).

Just to clarify: This is not an issue with a specific binding (in this case the Astro binding). I just used this for testing purposes because it's a small, stable binding than be installed and configured quickly. This issue also applies to other bindings and their config. 

To reproduce I installed the 'Astro' binding and created a `astro.things ` text file containing the following configuration:

```
Thing astro:sun:home        "VT_Astro_Sun"          @   "Virtual"       [ geolocation="6.524379,3.379206", interval=60 ] 
{
    Channels:
        Type rangeEvent : rise#event [
            offset=0
        ]
        Type rangeEvent : set#event [
            offset=0
        ]        
}
Thing astro:moon:home       "VT_Astro_Moon"         @   "Virtual"       [ geolocation="6.524379,3.379206", interval=60 ]
```

This works as expected and creates two Things in OpenHAB.

Next I comment out the 'VT_Astro_Moon' in the 'Thing' config and it's handler gets disposed and the Thing disappears from OpenHAB as expected.

When I remove the previously added comments to have OpenHAB (re)create the 'VT_Astro_Moon' thing nothing gets created.

I'm not sure if the problem lies with the original Thing not properly getting disposed or with the instantiation of the Thing/ThingHandler when I try to add it again.

I tested this on an OpenHAB build running on Windows 10 as well as within a Docker container on RancherOS. All builds were freshly installed and contained no other bindings or configurations other than what is there by default.

~~I will try to see if I can reproduce this on 2.4.0 and the 2.5.0-SNAPSHOT as well~~

EDIT: I was able to reproduce this behavior in 2.4.0 as well as the latest SNAPSHOT. The only ways around this issue are: 
- To rename the 'thing_id' part of the configuration. (`Thing <binding_id>:<type_id>:<thing_id>`)
  - OR-
- To restart the entire OpenHAB instance

title: [serial] dropdown of choices collapses to first selected port
body:
Currently running S1585, but this may go back to 2.4. I have only observed this using the zigbee and zwave bindings, but there have been reports in the forum where this occurs for other bindings. [Here's one for jeelink and zwave](https://community.openhab.org/t/snapshot-version-of-zwave-cannot-find-serial-port-after-oh-restart/73638/25?u=5iver). 

**To reproduce**
1) install the zwave and zigbee bindings with controllers for each, but don't configure yet
2) observe that the serial port dropdown for both bindings contain all ports
3) configure a port for zwave
4) observe that the serial prort dropdown for the zwave and zigbee bindings now only contain the port that had been selected for the zwave binding
5) after an OH restart, observe all ports are in the dropdown again for both bindings
6) configure a port for zigbee
7) observe the serial port dropdown for both bindings now only contain the port selected for zigbee

Possibly related, I also observe the zigbee binding losing it's serial port connection about once a day. The zigbee binding uses [gnu.io.SerialPort](https://github.com/openhab/org.openhab.binding.zigbee/blob/master/org.openhab.binding.zigbee/src/main/java/org/openhab/binding/zigbee/handler/ZigBeeSerialPort.java#L28) and zwave uses [org.eclipse.smarthome.io.transport.serial.SerialPort](https://github.com/openhab/org.openhab.binding.zwave/blob/master/src/main/java/org/openhab/binding/zwave/handler/ZWaveSerialHandler.java#L22). So, possibly a conflict in using the different transports?

More details can be found here (see issue 2)... https://github.com/openhab/org.openhab.binding.zwave/issues/1165. 

Note: After manually installing the bindings, the dropdowns have disappeared completely and allow free-text entries for the port. When doing the manual install, I only installed the openhab-core-io-transport-serial and openhab-core-config-discovery-usbserial features to resolve serial dependencies. However, zigbee still looses connection to its port at least once a day.

body: Observed on S1597, but very likely occurs on earlier post ESH reintegration snapshots too. With OH running on a Windows machine, scripts do not load at startup. After saving a script, the script is loaded. I've reproduced this in a test environment while troubleshooting the issue someone had [reported in the forum](https://community.openhab.org/t/jsr223-jython-simplified-rule-definition-similar-to-rules-dsl-and-universal-decorator/53252/172?u=5iver). I plan to investigate further.

title: Be sure to start the serial providers before the bindings using them
body:
It was discovered at least with the Z-Wave binding that at startup, the serial port is unknown by the openHAB serial abstraction. Just restarting the binding later solves the problem (the serial port is correctly identified).

https://github.com/openhab/org.openhab.binding.zwave/issues/1203

The Z-Wave binding handler factory bundle has a "immediate = true" property but it is not yet sure that it is the cause of the issue.

The current assumption is that the openHAB serial abstraction should be started with a higher priority, meaning with a start level < 80.

WDYT ?

title: USART serial availableForWrite() not working
body:
There’s a simple typo in the implementation of `USARTSerial::availableForWrite()`:

``` cpp
int USARTSerial::availableForWrite(void)
{
return HAL_USART_Available_Data(_serial);
}
int USARTSerial::available(void)
{
return HAL_USART_Available_Data(_serial);
}
```

https://github.com/spark/firmware/blob/develop/wiring/src/spark_wiring_usartserial.cpp#L69

It should probably be `HAL_USART_Available_Data_For_Write`. However, if I fix that and use it with code like:

``` cpp
        Serial.printlnf("%d", Serial1.availableForWrite());
        Serial1.println("01234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789");
        Serial.printlnf("%d", Serial1.availableForWrite());
```

The output is:

```
0
50
```

I’m unclear of how the function is supposed to work. Should it:
1. Return the number of bytes waiting to be written out from the buffer (0=empty send buffer), which is what it does.
2. Return the number of bytes you can write to the buffer without blocking, which would be SERIAL_BUFFER_SIZE - the value currently returned.

Thanks,
Rick

- This is important because the electron system firmware is compiled by default with `DEBUG_BUILD=y`, and when the application checksum is the same (as is the case when sleeping and waking up), the handshake process can be VERY short which means little data used.  When the application checksum is different, unnecessary data usage is occuring for each re-connection to the cloud.

- Part of this issue resolution could be choosing an antenna dedicated to the frequency used on that particular electron (i.e. U260 in 3G mode (UMTS) would only be 1900 MHz, whereas 2G mode (GSM) is 850 MHz which we could ignore in an antenna selection ).

title: [Electron] Application/System thread not blocking on calls to modem with SYSTEM_THREAD(ENABLED)
body:
SYSTEM_THREAD(ENABLED) is not blocking on calls to the modem, so the application thread doesn't wait for the modem to finish before going to the next instruction in user code.  Thus Cellular.on() and SLEEP_MODE_SOFTPOWEROFF will not work properly with threading enabled currently.

SYSTEM_THREAD(ENABLED);

void setup() {
}

  // we need to turn on the modem in SEMI_AUTOMATIC mode first, 
  // so that AT commands can be sent to turn it off

  // system will not wait for power on AT command sequence

title: Photon/P1 does not always recover from a WiFi channel switch / WiFi.ready() can return true with IP 0.0.0.0
body:
## Bug Report
According to the docs, WiFi.ready() returns true only if the device is connected to WiFi and has a valid IP address. My P1 based board connects to WiFi without problems initially. Then it loses network, and the code I have to restore WiFi is not triggered, because WiFi.ready() stil returns true.

I have narrowed down the cause to WiFi channel switching. Auto channel seems to be the default on many routers, so this affects many setups.

Initially, this bug report was about WiFi.ready() returning 'true' while the IP address was `0.0.0.0`, but this seems to be one of the symptoms of WiFi channel switching not being handled correctly.

### Expected Behavior

#### WiFi.ready()
WiFi.ready() returns true only if the P1 has a valid IP address, as described here:
https://docs.particle.io/reference/firmware/photon/#ready-

What should it do?
Return `false` if the IP address is `0.0.0.0`.

#### Channel switching
The photon should be able to switch seamlessly to a new WiFi channel if the router changes the channel.

### Observed Behavior

When I switch the WiFi channel on my router, the behavior of the photon is not consistent.
I see one of the following behaviors:

* Photon starts blinking green. Display shows WiFi.ready() returning false and IP address becoming 0.0.0.0. A short blue blink is followed by a white blink and then green blinking again and a successful reconnect.
* Photon starts flashing green, then switches to breathing green. WiFi.ready() stays true, but IP address becomes 0.0.0.0. Doesn't recover from this state. It's in limbo until a reboot.
* Hard fault SOS (1 blink).


### Analysis of the problem

In my application, I display WiFi status on a TFT display. It displays the IP address in light grey when connected and in dark grey when not connected (code below).

![2017-08-20 12 51 47](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1708921/29494587-dfb846a0-85ad-11e7-830b-b1f1f5ec7425.jpg)


```
void ControllerWiFiView::update(bool wifiConnected, char * const ipAddress)
{
    if(obj != nullptr){
        obj->clrScheme->fore = wifiConnected ? D4D_COLOR_LIGHT_GREY : D4D_COLOR_GREY;
        D4D_SetText(obj, ipAddress);
    }
}

void ControllerWiFiPresenter::update(){
#if BREWPI_USE_WIFI
    char ipAddressString[16];
    bool wifiConnected = WiFi.ready();
    piLink.ipAddressAsString(ipAddressString);
    view_.update(wifiConnected, ipAddressString);
#endif
}
```

I observe light grey with IP address 0.0.0.0. This means that it is possible for the P1 to get in a state where WiFi.ready() returns `true`, while the IP address is `0.0.0.0`.

I have connected a debugger and step debugged the code with Eclipse. This confirms that WiFi.ready() returns `false`.

I cannot fully step debug to the actual code that determines the ready status, because it seems to be a dynalib system call. But here is my analysis:

WiFi.ready() calls network_ready(..)
```
    bool ready(void) {
        return network_ready(*this, 0, NULL);
    }
```
Which is defined here:
```
DYNALIB_FN(4, system_net, network_ready, bool(network_handle_t, uint32_t, void*))
```
And results in:
```
bool network_ready(network_handle_t network, uint32_t param, void* reserved)
{
    return nif(network).ready();
}
```
Which seems to call `wifi.ready()`.

I think all the virtual functions eventually end up here (ManagedNetworkInterface class):
```
    bool ready() override
    {
        return (SPARK_WLAN_STARTED && WLAN_CONNECTED);
    }
```
So the volatile status byte WLAN_CONNECTED is used.
It is set to `1` on a successful DHCP connect. 
It is set to '0' on 
`ManagedNetworkInterface::notify_disconnected()`
`ManagedNetworkInterface::disconnect()`
`ManagedNetworkInterface::off()`
In `system_network_internal.cpp`

My guess is that the notify_disconnect never happens in this case. I have set a breakpoint on all 3 write occurrences that set WLAN_CONNECTED to zero. We'll have to wait until it happens again.

### Steps to Reproduce
Log in to your router, change the WiFi channel.

I am running the latest 0.7.0-rc.3 system firmware, compiled with arm-non-eabi-gcc 0.5.3.
I also use:
```
SYSTEM_MODE(MANUAL);
SYSTEM_THREAD(ENABLED);
```

However, this behavior has been present with older versions of the system firmware too (0.5.3). It seems to occur less often on 0.7.0 though.

### References

Full firmware I am running:
https://github.com/BrewPi/firmware

Code to maintain WiFi connection (it can switch between WiFi and Serial):
https://github.com/BrewPi/firmware/blob/master/app/controller/PiLink.cpp#L80

Code to display WiFi status on display:
https://github.com/BrewPi/firmware/blob/master/platform/spark/modules/eGUI_screens/ConnectivityDisplay.cpp#L42

### Possible workaround
Instead of `WiFi.ready()` use `WiFi.ready() && WiFi.localIP()[0]==0)`.

Related forum topic (from 2014): https://community.particle.io/t/wifi-ready-not-working/6627

title: 0.8.0-rc.1 Photon: Particle.connected does not sense lost internet
Particle.keepAlive() API does not work
Bad WiFi reception causes WiFi.RSSI() to return 2 and a following WiFi.disconnect() to SOS with stack overflow
body:
In an attempt to investigate the terrible WiFi reliability and TCP reliability that has gone unfixed for at least 6 months now, I wrote some test code and stumbled upon very bad behavior when handling WiFi. Please stop ignoring this Particle. Read the full bug report below, because it is complex. It is affecting my customers. I bought a lot of units from you, cores, photons, P1's. As a long time customer, I'm very disappointed that a WiFi IOT product does not take bug reports about bad WiFi reliability more seriously.
## Bug Report ### Expected Behavior When WiFi connection is lost due to bad reception: - LED stops breathing green - WiFi.ready() returns false - WiFi is restarted ### Observed Behavior To test why TCP stopped working sometimes, I wrote 2 pieces of test code: - A python script to show what is printed over serial and to send a TCP message every second and to print TCP replies (tic-toc) - A Photon app to reply to TCP requests and report system status. #### The python script - Prints anything received over serial to terminal in GREEN text - Prints a message in RED when it sends a TCP message to the photon - Prints a message in BLUE when it receives are TCP message from the photon - Sends a TCP message every second #### The firmware on the photon - Starts a TCP server on port 6666 - Listens for clients - Runs a system thread - Handles TCP server start/stop with network event handlers setting a flag (relying on WiFi.ready() seems to be unreliable) - Prints to serial: WiFi.ready(), IP address, RSSI, TCP client connected, millis() - Prints DEBUG logs - Prints SerialLogHandler traceLog(LOG_LEVEL_TRACE); #### Behavior Before adding `if(signal == 2){` block - TCP tic/toc just seems to stop at some point and doesn't recover - WiFi.RSSI returns 2 when problems start. This is triggered by bad reception. Doesn't recover after reception restored. In an attempt to fix I added the block to handle RSSI of 2. - When the code block is triggered, WiFi.disconnect() causes an SOS with 13 blinks: stack overflow. - Device never returns from SOS, stays in SOS until hard reset. ## Bug Report

### Expected Behavior

Stay connected without an external battery.

### Observed Behavior

Upgrading to 0.8.0-rc7 has made it so our units no longer stay connected when booted off the power supply. We are using a regulated lab 5V supply rated well in excess of 5A.

This occurs whether the firmware was compiled for 0.7.0 or 0.8.0-rc4 (-rc7 is not available right now as an option in Particle Dev).

title: attachInterrupt() fails for pin D7 on Boron
body:
## Bug Report

### Expected Behavior

attachInterrupt(D7, myFunc, RISING) == true;

### Observed Behavior

attachInterrupt(D7, myFunc, RISING) == false;

### Steps to Reproduce

Using firmware 1.4.0, attempt to attach an interrupt to D7 on a Boron device and it will return false.

I'm almost positive this is due to legacy (electron specific if my research is correct) code in spark_wiring_interrupts.cpp which has this catch in the attachInterrupt() definition:

```
#if Wiring_Cellular == 1
  /* safety check that prevents users from attaching an interrupt to D7
   * which is shared with BATT_INT_PC13 for power management */
  if (pin == D7) return false;
#endif 
```
And while the docs for the Electron clearly label this pin as off limits for that device, the docs for Boron state:

```
All A and D pins (including TX, RX, and SPI) on Gen 3 (mesh) devices can be used for interrupts...
```
I'm fairly certain Wiring_Cellular still gets set on the Boron though.

title: Feature request: Put modem in standby without sleeping MCU
body:
### Request:
On some of the sleep modes available for the electron it is possible to set the SLEEP_NETWORK_STANDBY flag. This will put the modem in standby mode before putting the MCU to sleep.

It would be really handy to put the modem in standby mode but keep the MCU active. This would drastically reduce power consumption and when data is ready to be sent a connection to the operator can quickly be made.

### Some background information:
I built a solar powered weather station also measuring wind speed. Anemometer rotations are counted using a counter IC. Every 5 seconds the Electron is woken from sleep, reads and clears the counter and goes back to sleep. After 5 minutes of collecting data, the average, maximum and minimum wind speed are calculated. The modem is turned on and the results are published to a web server. Then the modem is turned off and the Electron goes back to sleep. The cycle repeats.

The problem with this approach it that it takes at least 20 seconds to connect to the cellular network and a lot of data is used in the process.

The alternative is not to sleep at all, but this is really power hungry which is a problem for a solar powered system.

### My  proposed solution:
Put the modem in standby mode. When the Electron is woken up every 5 seconds to read the counter the modem should remain in standby mode. When 5 minutes passed, the modem should come out of standby mode, publish data and then go back to standby.

Currently the modem only remains in standby while the Electron is sleeping.

Any advice on how to achieve this would be appreciated.

title: Send endlessly returning zero
body:
_This bug is top priority because it blocks deep update. Must resolve ASAP._

Often, but inconsistently, OTA updates will fail, usually right at the beginning.  When they fail, the LED turns magenta and simply freezes, then after 20 seconds, the Core gives up on the TCP socket and reconnects to the Cloud.

Here is more detail on the conversation between Core and Cloud during this type of failure and the code path through the communication library, firmware, and common library.
- The Spark Cloud sends an `UPDATE_BEGIN` message, which the Core handles [here](https://github.com/spark/core-communication-lib/blob/master/src/spark_protocol.cpp#L1005).
- The Cloud successfully receives the [empty acknowledgement](https://github.com/spark/core-communication-lib/blob/master/src/spark_protocol.cpp#L1009).
- The LED turns magenta inside the [`prepare_for_firmware_update` callback](https://github.com/spark/core-communication-lib/blob/master/src/spark_protocol.cpp#L1016) (implemented [here](https://github.com/spark/core-firmware/blob/master/src/spark_utilities.cpp#L431) in core-firmware, mostly delegated [here](https://github.com/spark/core-common-lib/blob/master/SPARK_Firmware_Driver/src/hw_config.c#L1478) in core-common-lib)
- The `UPDATE_BEGIN` handler [attempts to send](https://github.com/spark/core-communication-lib/blob/master/src/spark_protocol.cpp#L1023) the `UPDATE_READY` message
- Our blocking send implementation [times out after 20 seconds](https://github.com/spark/core-communication-lib/blob/master/src/spark_protocol.cpp#L221)
- That's because the [CC3000 `send` call](https://github.com/spark/core-firmware/blob/master/src/spark_utilities.cpp#L382) is endlessly returning zero, meaning it is neither sending anything nor alerting us to an error condition.

This may (not necessarily, but worth testing) be a result of our [removal of `select` back in February](https://github.com/spark/core-firmware/commit/2988e1112bf21efa531de89c2229b27543b702fa) to speed up OTA updates.

@satishgn Please stop all other work and fix this as soon as possible. If we have a fix by tomorrow (Monday) morning (in Minneapolis) then we may be able to deploy deep update this week. Otherwise it will probably have to wait until I (@towynlin) arrive in San Francisco in a week.

If anyone from the Spark community wants to help with debugging this one, please do! **All hands on deck!** We want to deploy the TI patch for CFOD, which we're calling "deep update", but that must wait on a fix for this issue.

title: Time zone not updated immediately
Photon long handshake => malformed description message
body:
On prototype photon boards, the cloud handshake often takes many seconds longer than expected. After some digging into this, we found that the device service is receiving a malformed CoAP description message. Here are two examples in xxd format:

```
0000000: d5ff 267d 9521 7b22 6622 3a5b 5d2c 2276  ..&}.!{"f":[],"v
0000010: 223a 7b7d 7d                             ":{}}
```

```
0000000: 2159 bc92 3fe9 7b22 6622 3a5b 5d2c 2276  !Y..?.{"f":[],"v
0000010: 223a 7b7d 7d                             ":{}}
```

In both cases the first 6 bytes are malformed, whereas everything after that is fine. In particular, the device service is crying foul when the most significant 2 bits of the first byte of the message (the CoAP version) are anything other than `01`, the only value allowed by the CoAP spec.

As can be seen obviously in [the code](https://github.com/spark/firmware/blob/feature/hal/communication/src/spark_protocol.cpp#L612-L617), the first 2 bytes should always be `0x61 0x45` and the sixth byte should always be `0xff`. The 3rd, 4th, and 5th bytes may be anything.

I suspect one of two things is happening. Either:
- the RTOS on the Photon is interleaving access to `queue` so that those bytes are being overwritten (e.g., by a `blocking_receive`) before we finish the `blocking_send` of the description message, or
- whatever resides immediately before `queue` in memory is writing beyond the end with pointer math and the buffer overrun is not being caught by the compiler

Low priority for the moment (since handshake always eventually succeeds), but @m-mcgowan take a look when you're in the mood for some low level debugging.

title: spark protocol: events with composite names only work for the handler in slot 0.
body:
A composite event name is one containing a slash, such as "test/event1". When a composite event name is received, the receive buffer is modified in place from the CoAP data to produce the full name. However, this only works correctly for the first iteration of the loop and so only for the event handler at slot 0 - subsequent iterations of the loop over the remaining handlers (https://github.com/spark/firmware/blob/feature/hal/communication/src/spark_protocol.cpp#L1063) don't compare the handler filter with the full event name, but just the name component up to the first slash,  e.g."test". Since the handler filter ("test/event1") is more specific than the apparent name of the event ("test"), the handler isn't invoked.

The fix is to decode the event name and data once outside of the loop, and then use that info in a loop to check for a match against each handler.

title: Wi-Fi automatically connects to AP after WiFi.on()
body:
Hi there,

In general, `WiFi.on()` would not connect photon to an AP until `WiFi.connect()` is called. If I make the photon out of the AP range, it will always try to connect to the AP. Then I turn off the WiFi using `WiFi.off()` and then turn on it again by `WiFi.on()`, photon launched to connect to the AP immediately , instead of staying at fading blue. I.e.:

case 1.WiFi.on() -> stay at fading blue
case 2.WiFi.on() -> WiFi.connect() -> connect failed and WiFi.off() -> WiFi.on() -> connect to AP immediately.

Is the case 2 normal or a bug?

I looked into the code, I think it is probably caused by not clearing the wlan watch dog(`CLR_WLAN_WD()`) when calling WiFi.off(), so that upon the WiFi.on() is called the watch dog fired in function `manage_network_connection()`. Am I right?

If this is not a potential bug, I will close this issue. Waiting for your respond.

title: Feature/arduino compatibility regression
body:
Attempts to restore 0.6.0-style arduino compatibility as outlined by issue #1278 

In a nutshell:

- the default is 0.6.0 Arduino compatibility - let's call this partial compatibility. 
- applications and libraries include "Arduino.h" to define `ARDUINO` and bring in many more additional defines to complete the Arduino API.  We'll call this full compatibility. 


## Mixing libraries that require partial and full Arduino compatibility

Libraries that require full Arduino compatibility may include Arduino.h in their library header file, while libraries that depend on partial compatibility (because they themselves define missing symbols) don't include Arduino.h.  If a library requiring partial compatibility is included after one requiring full compatibility then the partial compatibility library may break, since Arduino symbols that it's not expecting will be defined. 

The workaround for this is to include all libraries requiring partial compatibility before libraries requiring full compatibility in the application file.

title: [USB] Fixes an issue with Serial when receiving consecutive multiple 64-byte transmissions from Host
body:
### Problem

With RX queue full, the device NAKs OUT (Host->Device) transfers. With `bInterval` set to `0` (1 ms) this causes the device to spend too much time in USB interrupt, not giving any processing time to the application/system thread to consume RX queue. For some reason CDC driver on OSX doesn't attempt to send any data after about 300 NAKed transfers. Closing/re-opening the port doesn't help either.

### Solution

Set `bInterval` to a maximum value (16 ms) on OUT endpoint to give enough time for the device to consume RX queue and not send too many NAKs to Host.

We should probably add some workaround as well: e.g. count the number of NAKs sent and silently drop incoming data after a certain threshold instead of NAKing it. Even though this is OSX driver's fault. :face_with_head_bandage:

### Steps to Test

The bug is easily reproducible on OSX when setting WPA Enterprise credentials over Serial. A simple copy-paste of a certificate (e.g. CA) will not complete and get stuck somewhere half-way through.

title: Fix endless IWDG reset loop
body:
### Problem

In order to minimize usage of the DCT in the bootloader, the firmware now uses backup registers to store system flags (see https://github.com/spark/firmware/pull/1325). This poses a problem when firmware is downgraded from 0.7.0-rc.1: bootloader enables IWDG and sets a flag in the backup registers, but an older firmware is unable to detect that IWDG is running since it expects IWDG flag to be set in the DCT. This causes the device to reset every 5 seconds.

### Solution

Do not enable IWDG if currently flashed firmware has a version number lower than 0.7.0-rc.1. This gives user a possibility to downgrade the bootloader properly.

### Steps to Test

1. Set all module versions to 200 (0.7.0-rc.1) in [system_module_version.mk](https://github.com/spark/firmware/blob/fix/disable_iwdg/modules/shared/system_module_version.mk).
2. Compile and flash all system parts **and bootloader** to the device.
3. Flash 0.6.2 firmware via DFU. The device should work normally without resetting unexpectedly.

title: [Electron] Fixes missing URCs for received data during TX or RX socket operations
body:
### Problem

We've been getting reports of times when devices seem to stop being able to receive data.  They seem to recover after the device exhausts its retries (about 78 seconds) and reconnects to the Cloud.  This has been a tricky bug to nail down, but it appears to be a corner case in how the cellular modem reports URCs, or in this case, doesn't report them.

The error condition occurs with the following sequence.  We start with the RX buffer is empty.  We receive some data, and the modem notifies us of this pending data via URC (Unsolicited Response Code). When we go to read that data from the modem, if we received more data concurrently, no further URC is generated after the data is received, or after the read completes.  The error case can occur during a write operation as well (receiving data while we are sending data).  We normally rely on URCs to allow us to receive status from the modem asynchronously and avoid polling it for status, which allows it to enter low power mode as well.

### Solution

After extensive testing it was discovered that a forced poll of the socket (AT+USORF=0,0 for UDP and AT+USORD=0,0 for TCP) after all read and write operations was necessary to mitigate this corner case when we don't receive URCs naturally for received data.

There will be a 40 ms delay to poll the modem for pending data after every packet sent and received.  This cost in time comes with the reward of reliability.

### Steps to Test

- `TEST=wiring/no_fixture`
- Extensive internal testing has shown this fix is very reliable. In general what is needed is a fast echo server to send lots of traffic to the device, and for the device to also echo that data back to the server. The server should also let the device repeatedly catch-up and process all messages so that the RX buffer can start from 0 many times.

title: [LTE/Electron] Fixes software Timer()'s halting after millis() overflows (every 49.7 days)
[LTE/Electron] bug fixes and enhancements
body:
### Problem

Several LTE bugs have been found that all revolve around socket AT commands being prone to various types of failure.  See below.

### Solution(s)

#### Fixes incorrect handling of socket send when lost signal recovers during 2nd try
    
- If signal was lost before socket send, first command would timeout, during retry if signal was restored the first command would send and return OK instead of the second command requiring a PROMPT.  We would return a socket error instead of signaling data was sent OK.  This caused a network teardown and reconnection unnecessarily.
- Also adjusts the timeouts for various commands used during socket send operations.

#### Changes eDRX mode command so that it fully indicates it is disabled
    
- Despite eDRX mode being disabled via CEDRXS=0, it would still indicate \r\n+CEDRXS: 2, ... \r\n
- Now with CEDRXS=3,2 it will respond as fully disabled \r\n+CEDRXS:\r\n

#### Fixes LTE AT command interface failing when sending data with no cell signal, and more... [ch26915]
    
- If signal was lost before data sent, the AT interface would hang until the modem was reset.  This process would take around 10 minutes.
- Added checks for network registration before certain commands: USOST, USOCO, USOWR, USOCL to prevent AT interface hanging.  Unfortunately it still takes 20-30s before network registration updates, so we can still stall on these commands at times.
- Timeouts were reduced as much as possible per AT command manuals to speed up recovery process when AT interface fails.  Some timeouts were optimized for UDP usage.
- Additional checks for AT interface being available were added before long timeout commands.
- Improvements to power off routine added by using the PWR_UC pin and checking for V_INT voltage to drop.
- 10ms delay changed to 1ms delay in main parsing loop to speed up processing of many commands.
- Removed 50ms delay in socket send functions (TCP & UDP) which should also speed up communication.
- CREG?/CGREG?/CEREG? polling sped up considerably from 15s delays between tries to 10ms (1500x faster in certain cases). Time to register now on 2G/3G/LTE can be <4s for a warm boot and <9s for a cold boot.

#### Fixes LTE devices remaining disconnected until reset when connecting with no signal [ch26919]
    
- If the modem starts up with the factory default URAT setting of 7,8 (Cat-M1 & Cat-NB1) and is not able to initially connect to a Cat-M1 network, it will start scanning for Cat-NB1 networks and not return to scanning for Cat-M1 networks. In this case, it will be unable to connect to a Cat-M1 network until the cellular modem is power cycled after 5 minutes.
- Solution is to disable Cat-NB1 RAT and only use Cat-M1 RAT by default.

#### Fixes LTE/Electron AT command replay issue [ch26922]
    
- If the AT interface fails, commands sent to the modem can be replayed when it is power cycled and reset due to the circular buffer not being cleared completely.
- This resolves the issue by resetting all indexes used in the circular buffer to 0 when the serial pipe is effectively closed.

#### Make UPSD/USPDA/USPND timeouts proper (UPSDA was being short changed in deactivate()

#### Fixes PWM tests calculations and speeds up PWM wiring/no_fixture test

### Steps to Test

- Run `wiring/no_fixture` tests
- Simulate no signal by removing the antenna
    - and sending data after 5 seconds, wait for AT commands to fail, replace antenna after 30 seconds, unit should recover after about 60 seconds from when data was sent.
    - and sending data after 5 seconds, wait for AT commands to fail, reset the device, unit should boot up again and try to register.  (failing case would get stuck in listening mode repeatedly due to the AT command replay issue)
    - and sending data after 40 seconds (unit should already be indicating no signal and no network connection), AT commands should not fail as all offending commands should be avoided with CEREG? checks, replace antenna, unit should recover in about 30 seconds from when data was sent.
    - and sending data immediately, and replace antenna after first USOST command observed, unit should recover without issue and keep communicating.
    - and sending data immediately, and replace antenna after second USOST command observed, unit should usually recover without issue and keep communicating.
    - and cold boot the unit, and observe it will now toggle between CEREG: 2,0 and CEREG: 2,2.  After replacing the antenna it will connect almost immediately.
- Ensure URAT? responds with +URAT: 7 instead of +URAT: 7,8
- Attempt to force URAT=7,8 to check again that system will fix this default situation
```c
SYSTEM_MODE(SEMI_AUTOMATIC);
SYSTEM_THREAD(ENABLED);
void setup() {
    cellular_on(NULL);
    cellular_command(NULL, NULL, 1000, "AT+URAT=7,8\r\n");
    Particle.connect();
}
```

title: [Electron/LTE] disables all eDRX AcT types [ch32051]
body:
### Problem

eDRX is enabled by default on production u-Blox modules, and it causes a variable lag in the network data transmissions.  We have previously disabled it, but not entirely.

### Solution

Scan for and disable each eDRX AcT type, and reset the modem if disabling is required or an error occurs.

>**Note:** When disabling eDRX mode, the modem needs to be reset to clear eDRX behavior in the cellular network.  This will cause a one time ~30s reconnection delay after OTA updating the new firmware.

>**Note:** When eDRX mode is enabled, TX on the device temporarily allows the network to RX faster.  For example, if the device published every 2 minutes and we asynchronous tried to read a Particle Variable every ~5 seconds, the device would up timing out 2-3 times in a row and succeeding 2-3 times in a row repeatedly.  This affects OTA updates as well.  An OTA update might never start until the device pings the Cloud and reduces the RX timing in the network.  Because of this, devices with this behavior that are remote in the field might need special care in updating them remotely, Ex. a script that repeatedly tries OTA updating every 30 seconds for 30 minutes.

### Steps to Test

🔗 [Electron/LTE firmware compiled for this PR-1762, v1.1.0-rc.2.  Tinker included but not required.](https://www.dropbox.com/s/gox036vwxp51iok/particle_device-os%401.1.0-rc.2-pr-1762.zip?dl=1)

Manual testing required:
1. Flash LTE device with this system firmware and tinker
2. Make a function call `particle call <device> digitalwrite D7,LOW`
3. It should return 1 if successful
4. Repeat every 30 seconds for 10 or more attempts

⚠️ Should you need to for testing purposes, you may enable eDRX mode with the following commands:

```c
sendFormated("AT+CEDRXS=2,2,\"1001\"\r\n"); waitFinalResp();
sendFormated("AT+CEDRXS=2,3,\"1001\"\r\n"); waitFinalResp();
sendFormated("AT+CEDRXS=2,4,\"1001\"\r\n"); waitFinalResp();
sendFormated("AT+CEDRXS=2,5,\"1001\"\r\n"); waitFinalResp();
```

title: [Gen 3] Fixes various issues caused by the gateway reset
body:
### Problem

Mesh devices may be unable to connect to the cloud or appear to be connected but can neither send nor receive data to/from the cloud under certain conditions.

### Solution

1. OpenThread version we've upgraded to in the end of January moved SLAAC functionality into its core and enabled it by default, which interfered with our own SLAAC logic. A PR was submitted later to the OpenThread repo to make this configurable, so for now we are simply pulling in that PR and disable SLAAC: https://github.com/particle-iot/openthread/commit/ea382ea6002ce41af4151bac64e26b36a1e3cb49
2. Under certain conditions (see 'Steps to Test' to replicate) mesh devices don't notice that the gateway has been reset. This is resolved by artificially publishing a prefix with `preferred` flag set to 0 (which means that the addresses generated from this prefix should be 'DEPRECATED' but may still be used for communications), waiting for this change to propagate through the network and then re-publishing with proper `preferred` set to 1, so that the device can receive events from OpenThread about a potential change in upstream connection availability and explicitly check their cloud connection state by issuing a ping.
3. When changing the state of IP addresses on OpenThread interface, make sure that events are being fired, so that system level subscribers may understand that there is a potential change in connection availability.
4. Make sure that `Pref::1/PrefLen` address is always generated (instead of a random one) from the prefix announced by the gateway itself no matter the current role (child or router).

### Steps to Test

The easiest way to test this is to create a mesh network of 3 devices.

1. Power down all devices
2. Power up non-gateway devices
3. Make sure that one of them becomes the leader (for now take a look at the logs for that)
4. Power on the gateway device
5. Wait until all three are connected to the cloud and are breathing cyan
6. Power off the gateway device for about a minute or so. The other two devices should stay breathing cyan (occasionally you might see some blinks due to ping timeouts and session resumption)
7. Power the gateway back on BEFORE the other devices start blinking green
8. All three should connect to the cloud. The non-gateway devices should not go through blinking green state.
9. Make sure you may reach your non-gateway devices from the cloud (e.g. `particle nyan`)
10. Wait for some minutes, you should still be able to reach your non-gateway devices and they should be breathing cyan

Steps 9 - 10 should fail on `develop` and should work correctly with this PR.
